title: Nagel’s Bat Argument — the first-person point of view
when: Thomas Nagel’s essay “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” appeared in The Philosophical Review in October 1974 and was reprinted in Mortal Questions (1979), amid debates over whether mental life could be reduced to brain processes.
people: Thomas Nagel; philosophers of mind debating materialist and reductionist explanations.
origin: Late-twentieth-century Anglo-American analytic philosophy, especially philosophy of mind and debates about scientific objectivity.
idea: Nagel asks whether an outside, third-person description can capture what an experience is like for the creature having it. A bat’s echolocation makes the gap vivid: we can study its sensory system and behavior, yet Nagel doubts that these facts alone let humans grasp the bat’s own point of view. He uses this example to argue that conscious experience has a subjective character that standard reductions of mind to physical or functional descriptions may leave unexplained. This is not a proof that consciousness is supernatural, that science is useless, or that physicalism is false. Nagel’s challenge is that an adequate account must take the first-person perspective seriously, while finding concepts capable of relating it to objective explanation.
relevance: The argument remains a touchstone for consciousness research: brain and behavioral data may be essential without settling what experience feels like. For animals and AI, it separates evidence of information processing from the harder question of whether there is something it is like to be the system.
